li.a: Yahoo News: Southport stabbing, everything we know about the attack as Axel Rudakubana is handed his sentence
Al Jazeera: UK teenager pleads guilty to killing three girls in Southport knife attack
UPI, published by Yahoo News: Axel Rudakubana pleads guilty to dance school stabbings
Rolling Stone, published by Yahoo News: Teen sentenced to 52 years for murdering three girls at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class
The Telegraph, published by Yahoo News: Starmer says the state failed in its ultimate duty to protect the Southport victims
The Guardian: Southport murderer bought weapons and ricin-making equipment two years before attack
GOV.UK: Prevent learning review, Axel Muganwa Rudakubana
The Southport Inquiry: Report, Volume 1, 13 April 2026

content.p: On the morning of 29 July 2024, a 17-year-old walked into a Taylor Swift-themed holiday workshop for children in Southport, Merseyside, and began stabbing the girls gathered there. Bebe King, aged six, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, aged seven, died at the scene. Alice da Silva Aguiar, aged nine, died in hospital the following day. Eight other children and two adults were wounded.

The attacker was Axel Rudakubana. On 20 January 2025, the first day of what was to be a four-week trial at Liverpool Crown Court, he pleaded guilty to every one of the 16 charges against him. Three days later he received a life term with a minimum of 52 years. The case did not end there. It set off riots in towns across the country, and it led to a public inquiry whose report, published in April 2026, concluded that no public body had taken responsibility for the danger he posed.
content.h2: A boy already known to the authorities
content.p: Rudakubana was born in Cardiff to parents who had come to Britain from Rwanda, and he lived in Banks, a village north-east of Southport. His parents are Christians, UPI reported. He had come to the attention of several agencies in 2019, around the time he turned 13, after what local safeguarding officials described as increasing anxiety and social isolation. The Guardian reported that he was excluded from Range High School in October 2019 for taking a knife into school and that he returned two months later and attacked a child with a hockey stick.

The official inquiry later described 11 December 2019, the day of that assault, as a watershed. In its account he had brought weapons to his former school intending to kill a particular pupil he believed had bullied him, and, when that was impossible, assaulted another pupil at random. The inquiry's chair, Sir Adrian Fulford, wrote that this should have led every agency involved to conclude that the boy posed a high risk of harm to others. Lancashire police dealt with him several times between October 2019 and May 2022, including five calls from his own family about his behaviour, the Guardian reported. He had also had contact with the courts, youth justice, social services and mental health services, Home Secretary Yvette Cooper said in a statement quoted by Yahoo News.

Prevent is the government's scheme to stop terrorist violence, as the Telegraph described it. A learning review commissioned by the Home Office's Homeland Security Group and Counter Terrorism Policing Headquarters, and later published on GOV.UK, set out the three occasions on which Rudakubana was referred to it.

The first came from a teacher on 5 December 2019. The teacher reported that he had been excluded from his previous school for carrying a knife and had searched online for mass school shootings using his school account. After officers spoke to him about the searches, the case was closed on 31 January 2020, the review said, on the view that there were no counter-terrorism concerns and that other agencies were already supporting him. The second came from his previous school on 1 February 2021, after a pupil showed the school social media posts by Rudakubana; the review said the school was concerned and felt he was being radicalised. It was closed on 17 February 2021. The third came on 26 April 2021, when a teacher saw internet tabs open in a lesson showing a search for "London Bomb", and noted a strong interest in the Israel-Palestine conflict, MI5 and the IRA. It was closed on 10 May 2021.

The reviewer found a high level of compliance with the rules in force at the time. Even so, the review said, the officers' subjective judgements were the problem, and Rudakubana should have been referred to Channel. It found weaknesses in how risk was assessed where no coherent ideology was present, and in how repeat referrals were treated.

A week before the attack, on 22 July, Rudakubana booked a taxi under the false name "Simon" to take him to his old school, the Guardian reported. Detectives believed the timing was no coincidence, because the school was due to break up for the summer ten minutes after the booking. His father pleaded with him not to go and the teenager went back into the house.

On 29 July he took a taxi from Banks to the dance studio on Hart Street. According to police accounts reported by the Guardian, the room held 26 girls aged between six and 11, who were making bracelets and singing. He entered at 11.45 a.m., fifteen minutes before parents were due to collect the children, and screams were heard within 30 seconds. Police called it a planned, premeditated attempt at mass murder, not a random act. They said Bebe and Elsie were so badly hurt that they had no chance of survival, and that Alice ran outside after being stabbed but died in hospital the next morning. When officers arrived, he was standing over one victim and dropped his knife when ordered to.

Two adults who tried to stop him were hurt: Leanne Lucas, the class instructor, and a businessman, John Hayes. One Yahoo News account said both had heroically tried to prevent the attack. Rudakubana was arrested at the scene.

Detectives found a cache of weapons at his home and items for making ricin, the Guardian reported. The Guardian reported that he had bought equipment for it online in 2022, three years after he first came to the attention of the authorities, and that he used security software to hide his identity when buying weapons. They found no evidence that he used the poison. Six minutes before he left home on 29 July, he searched for a video of the stabbing of a bishop at a church in Sydney earlier that year, according to the same report.

Officials told the Guardian that his internet history showed an obsession with extreme violence, including the Rwandan genocide, and that his tablets held material on conflicts and massacres from several periods and countries. Police also found a PDF titled "Military Studies in the Jihad Against the Tyrants: The Al-Qaeda Training Manual", and the Guardian reported that he had downloaded an Al-Qaida study as early as 2021. Possessing the manual led to a terrorism charge; UPI said prosecutors withheld information about that charge for three months. Police Chief Constable Serena Kennedy said other documents showed a "long-standing obsession with violence, killing and genocide".

Not-guilty pleas had been entered for Rudakubana in December 2024 because he would not speak in court. On 20 January 2025, as the clerk read out each count, he answered "guilty" to all of them: three of murder, ten of attempted murder, possession of a knife, producing ricin, and possessing the al-Qaeda manual. The victims' families were not in court to hear it, because the change of plea was a surprise, and the judge apologised to them. Judge Julian Goose told the defendant that a sentence equivalent to life imprisonment was now inevitable.

Deputy Chief Crown Prosecutor Ursula Doyle said he had shown no sign of remorse and that the plea had spared the families a trial. She described a "meticulously planned rampage" by a teenager with a "sickening and sustained interest in death and violence".

On 23 January Mr Justice Goose sentenced him to life with a minimum of 52 years. The judge described a "pre-meditated attempt to commit indiscriminate mass murder", said his intention had been to "murder as many as he could", and added that he would probably never be released. He said the evidence did not show that Rudakubana intended an act of terrorism, but that the attack was equivalent to terrorist matters. He was not expected to receive a whole-life order, the Telegraph reported, because he was under 18 at the time. Southport's MP, Patrick Hurley, asked the Attorney General to review the sentence as too lenient.

Shortly after the murders, false reports spread online that the suspect was a Muslim and an asylum seeker. In fact he was a British citizen born in Cardiff. Disturbances broke out in Southport and spread across the country over six days, the largest wave of unrest in the UK since the 2011 riots, according to the Yahoo News account. Mosques and hotels housing asylum seekers were attacked. Prime Minister Keir Starmer blamed the violence on far-right thuggery, Al Jazeera reported. About 130 police officers were injured. Reports give different totals for the arrests: more than 1,500 according to Al Jazeera, and 1,280 by September, with 800 charged, according to the Yahoo News piece. The Telegraph's editorial argued that official silence in the first days had fed rumour and distrust.

On 20 January 2025 Home Secretary Yvette Cooper announced a public inquiry into how Rudakubana "came to be so dangerous" and why Prevent "failed to identify the terrible risk" he posed. Cooper said the Home Office had commissioned an urgent Prevent learning review during the summer, but that advice from the Crown Prosecution Service had limited what could be said while the case was pending. Starmer said there were "grave questions to answer as to how the state failed in its ultimate duty to protect these young girls". The Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called for a full account of who in government knew what, and when.

The Southport Inquiry, chaired by Sir Adrian Fulford, published the first volume of its report on 13 April 2026. It identified five overlapping fundamental problems: no organisation taking ownership of the risk he posed; poor information management and sharing; excusing his behaviour because of a perceived or diagnosed autism spectrum disorder; failure to oversee and intervene in his online behaviour; and the role of his parents. On the first, it said no agency would accept that it had the lead role in managing the risk to others, with the partial exception of the youth justice service during a referral order that ran from February 2020 to January 2021.

The chair called it significantly troubling that no public body had the responsibility to monitor, investigate and neutralise a risk of that size, and he said that the authorities' understanding of the boy shrank as the years went by. The report went on to chapters on the weapons he bought, his online activity and the response on the day, and it recorded the lasting physical and psychological harm to the surviving children and adults, as well as the families of Bebe, Elsie and Alice. Fulford wrote that he hoped the inquiry would stand as a turning point.
